ABSTRACT
The Panel on Food Additives and Nutrient Sources added to Food provides a scientific opinion re-evaluating the
safety of tocopherol-rich extract of natural origin (E 306), synthetic α-tocopherol (all-rac-α-tocopherol; dl-α-
tocopherol; E 307), synthetic γ-tocopherol (dl-γ-tocopherol; E 308) and synthetic δ-tocopherol (E 309). The
European Union’s Scientific Committee on Food did not set an Acceptable Daily Intake (ADI), but derived a
Tolerable Upper Intake Level (UL) for vitamin E of 300 mg/day for adults. The Joint FAO/WHO Expert
Committee on Food Additives (JECFA) derived an ADI of 0.15–2 mg/kg body weight (bw)/day for dl-α-
tocopherol. The acute oral toxicity of tocopherols is low. In both a 13-week and a chronic (16-month) oral
toxicity study, the No Observed Adverse Effect Level (NOAEL) was 125 mg/kg bw/day. The critical adverse
effect is prolonged coagulation time. There is no concern that tocopherols are genotoxic or carcinogenic. There
are insufficient data to address the reproduction and developmental toxicity. The Panel concluded that the
available data are too limited to establish an ADI for the tocopherols. However, taking into account that vitamin
E is widely consumed via human food, it is an essential nutrient and that the ULs are not exceeded in any
population group, except in children in one survey from only one country, α-tocopherol, for the reported uses
and use levels as a food additive, is not considered to be of safety concern. The Panel considered that the dataset
on tocopherol-rich extract, and γ- and δ-tocopherol was too limited to be included in the safety assessment of
tocopherols. Moreover, the Panel is aware that much lower concentration levels and fewer uses for γ- and δ-
tocopherol are reported in food than for α-tocopherol. Therefore, the Panel concluded that tocopherols (E 306–
E 309) are not of safety concern at the levels used in food.

Re-evaluation of tocopherols (E 306–E 309) as food additives
SUMMARY 1
Following a request from the European Commission to the European Food Safety Authority (EFSA), 2
the Scientific Panel on Food Additives and Nutrient Sources added to Food (ANS Panel) was asked to 3
provide a scientific opinion re-evaluating the safety of tocopherol-rich extract of natural origin 4
(E 306), synthetic α-tocopherol (all-rac-α-tocopherol; dl-α-tocopherol; E 307), synthetic γ-tocopherol 5
(dl-γ-tocopherol; E 308) and synthetic δ-tocopherol (E 309), which are used as antioxidants in foods to 6
inhibit the peroxidation of fats and lipids. 7
The Panel was not provided with a newly submitted dossier and based its evaluation on previous 8
evaluations, additional literature that has become available since then and data provided following a 9
public call for data. The Panel noted that not all of the original studies on which the previous 10
evaluations were based were available for re-evaluation by the Panel. 11
Tocopherols belong to the group of substances named vitamin E. Vitamin E is the collective term for a 12
family of structurally related substances, namely tocopherol- and tocotrienol-derivatives, that exhibit, 13
qualitatively, the biological activity of the naturally occurring d-α-tocopherol. Vitamin E is an 14
essential vitamin and is naturally present in plant-derived foods, particularly fruit and vegetables. 15
All tocopherols evaluated in this opinion are used as antioxidants in food, either individually or in 16
combination, and are authorised under Annex II of Regulation (EC) No 1333/2008 on food additives. 17

3. Biological and toxicological data 1064
Some toxicological studies were submitted to EFSA following a public call for data for the evaluation 1065
of the tocopherols (α-, γ- and δ-tocopherols and tocopherol-rich extract). These are detailed in the 1066
following sections. In the available database, all toxicological testing was carried out with dl- or d- 1067
forms of the tocopherols of interest. No l-forms of tocopherols were used in the available toxicological 1068
studies. 1069
It is assumed that α-tocopherol is representative of the other tocopherols and can be considered as a 1070
worst case, based on the fact that the body preferentially retains α-tocopherol, rather than any of the 1071
other tocopherol forms, and that α-tocopherol is the most biologically active. 1072
The present opinion reports, in brief, key data discussed in previous major reviews by the SCF, 1073
JECFA, EFSA, the EVM and the IOM, but generally does not describe them in detail, as these data 1074
have already been extensively reviewed by these bodies, and their interpretation with regard to 1075
toxicology are comparable. Previously unavailable data, which were subsequently submitted to EFSA 1076
following a public call for data, have been described in detail and the results are discussed in relation 1077
to findings of the major reviews. 1078
It should be noted that different forms of vitamin E are sometimes referred to in terms of international 1079
units (IU). The most biologically active antioxidant is d-α-tocopherol. Vitamin E activity is expressed 1080
as d-α-tocopherol equivalents. Where activity is given in IU, 1 IU of d-α-tocopherol is equivalent to 1081
0.67 mg. If the vitamin E is present in the form of dl-α-tocopherol (E 307), then 1 IU is equivalent to 1082
0.91 mg (EVM, 2003). 1083
Absorption, distribution, metabolism and excretion (ADME) and toxicological studies with α- 1084
tocopherol derivatives have been considered for the safety assessment of α-tocopherol: d-α-tocopheryl 1085
acetate,19 dl-α-tocopheryl acetate,20 d-α-tocopheryl poly(ethylene glycol) 1000 succinate,21 d-α- 1086
tocopheryl acid succinate22 and RRR-α-tocopheryl phosphate.23 The Panel considered that such esters 1087
would be hydrolysed following absorption and deliver α-tocopherol. 1088
3.1. Absorption, distribution, metabolism and excretion 1089
An EFSA public call for data did not indicate that any new relevant data are available on the 1090
toxicokinetics of tocopherol-rich extract, or α -, γ- or δ-tocopherols. The literature search revealed 1091
several sources relating to the toxicokinetics of tocopherols. 1092

Re-evaluation of tocopherols (E 306–E 309) as food additives
3.1.1. Absorption 1093
Absorption of the tocopherols from the gastrointestinal tract begins with emulsification with dietary 1094
lipids. Absorption of lipids together with the fat-soluble vitamins depends on biliary secretion of bile 1095
acids and salts, which aid the emulsification process, to form micelles with the hydrolysed fat. The 1096
micelles containing tocopherols are then absorbed by passive diffusion at the brush border enterocytes 1097
of the small intestine (Traber et al., 1986; IOM, 2000; SCF, 2003; EFSA, 2008). 1098
The proportion of tocopherol intake that is absorbed from the small intestine appears to depend on the 1099
intake. Traber et al. (1986) measured the absorption of tocopherol during constant infusions of saline 1100
and soybean oils containing vitamin E, using rats (seven animals, sex and strain not stated) cannulated 1101
at the thoracic lymph duct for lymph collection. The amount of tocopherol infused was estimated to 1102
provide approximately 100 mg/kg bw/day. The absorption of α-tocopherol was approximately 64 %. 1103
The results of this study also showed that the percentage of α-tocopherol absorbed decreased with the 1104
administration of large oral doses of vitamin E in rats. Traber et al. (1986) also found that the 1105
proportion of γ-tocopherol absorbed was approximately 51 %, and was not decreased by 1106
administration of large doses of α-tocopherol, even when the amount of α-tocopherol exceeded γ- 1107
tocopherol by more than 50-fold. The authors of this study concluded that this finding indicates that 1108
gastrointestinal absorption of α- and γ-tocopherol are independent (Traber et al., 1986). The SCF 1109
opinion (SCF, 2003) stated that the average absorption of vitamin E is 40–60 %, but did not cite the 1110
sources for this conclusion. 1111
Anwar et al. (2007) investigated vitamin E transport and absorption in male Sprague–Dawley rats and 1112
C57BL/6J mice using d-α-[H3]tocopherol. In this study, it was confirmed that absorption of vitamin E 1113
is primarily by secretion by the enterocytes into the lymphatics in the form of chylomicrons. This 1114
pathway of absorption is dependent on an exogenous lipid supply, oleic acid and microsomal 1115
triglyceride transfer protein. In the case of lower lipid supply, vitamin E is secreted with larger 1116
lipoproteins without the need for chylomicrons. The size of the lipoprotein with which vitamin E is 1117
secreted is, in turn, dependent on the concentration of oleic acid. Higher concentrations of oleic acid 1118

conclusion. 1943
The EVM report (EVM, 2003) also discusses a study conducted by Stephens et al. (1996), which was 1944
a double-blind, placebo-controlled study aimed at investigating the hypothesis that treatment with a 1945
high dose of α-tocopherol would reduce the subsequent risk of myocardial infarction and 1946
cardiovascular death in patients with established ischaemic heart disease. In this study, 2 002 male and 1947
female patients with proven coronary atherosclerosis were enrolled. Of these, 546 patients received 1948
800 IU vitamin E per day (537 mg as d-α-tocopherol/day), 489 received 400 IU vitamin E per day 1949
(268 mg as d-α-tocopherol/day) and 967 received identical placebo capsules. The median follow-up 1950
period was 1.5 years. Treatment with α-tocopherol significantly reduced the risk of composite 1951
cardiovascular death and non-fatal myocardial infarction by 47 % (p < 0.005). The reduction in this 1952
risk was mainly accounted for by the significantly reduced risk of non-fatal myocardial infarction by 1953
77 % (p < 0.005), which was apparent after approximately 200 days of treatment with α-tocopherol. 1954
There was also an apparent, non-statistically significant, excess of cardiovascular deaths in the 1955
treatment group (p < 0.61), but the study authors noted that these events tended to occur early on in the 1956
study, perhaps before the treatment had had any effect. They also speculated that these might be 1957
chance findings or reflect a difference in biological events leading to the deaths, compared with those 1958
leading to non-fatal myocardial infarction. The EVM report (EVM, 2003) concluded that this result 1959
and the one from the Meydani et al. (1998) study, confirm the NOAEL of 537 mg d-α-tocopherol 1960
equivalents per day. 1961
Diplock (1995) concluded that there is evidence to suggest that vitamin E can exacerbate the blood 1962
coagulation defect of vitamin K deficiency caused by malabsorption or anticoagulant therapy, and 1963
suggested that high vitamin E intake is contraindicated in these subjects. An example of this was 1964
exhibited in a study conducted by Corrigan and Ulfers (1981), in which 12 adult cardiology patients 1965
(eight male and four female) that were being prescribed warfarin on a long-term basis (mean of 6.2 1966
years of treatment) consented to take supplemental vitamin E orally. Patients took either 100 or 400 IU 1967
(equivalent to 67 or 268 mg) of α-tocopherol per day for four weeks. Blood samples were collected 1968
monthly for five months before the vitamin E supplementation commenced, and then weekly during 1969
the supplementation period. Fifty adult patients, without known liver disease or vitamin K deficiency, 1970
served as controls. It was shown that the effect of warfarin was intensified when administered along 1971
with vitamin E; for example, prothrombin time was statistically significantly increased in the vitamin 1972
E-treated patients compared with controls (Corrigan and Ulfers, 1981). 1973
However, the SCF report (SCF, 2003) included studies on healthy humans, which showed that there 1974
was no adverse effect on platelet aggregation or adhesion when supplements of up to 800 mg α- 1975
tocopherol equivalents (1 200 IU) were taken (Farrell and Bieri, 1975; Tsai et al., 1978). Also, in the 1976
study by Kitagawa and Mino (1989; further details in Section 3.1.2), 19 healthy male students did not 1977
show any signs of toxicity or effects on thyroid, liver or kidney function, coagulation activity or 1978
immunoglobulin levels while taking 600 mg (900 IU) d-α-tocopherol per day for three months. 1979
Studies, such as those by Boaz et al. (2000), Lippman et al. (2009) and Leppala et al. (2000a), provide 1980
evidence for vitamin E having no adverse or beneficial effects on cardiovascular disease. Boaz et al. 1981
(2000) specifically investigated the effect of high doses of vitamin E on cardiovascular disease 1982
outcomes in haemodialysis patients (n = 196; 40–75 years old, male and female) with pre-existing 1983
cardiovascular disease. Patients were given supplements containing either 800 IU vitamin E per day or 1984
the placebo for two months, and followed up for a median of 519 days. Primary outcomes, myocardial 1985
infarction (fatal and non-fatal), ischaemic stroke, peripheral vascular disease and unstable angina, as 1986
well as secondary outcomes, such as total mortality and mortality related to cardiovascular disease, 1987
were monitored for associations with vitamin E supplementation. It was found that a total of 15 (16 %) 1988
